edges.relationship: Scott argues that Stone’s unequal standards marginalize women’s history and exclude it from defining standards for historical scholarship (1985).
edges.evidence_note: Scott concedes that his treatment of the two books was generally fair; her criticism concerns his framing and unequal criteria.

edges.relationship: Replying to Scott, Stone defends reciprocal standards for studying men and women together while apologizing for the tone of his commandments (1985).
edges.evidence_note: A substantive disagreement within the same exchange, not a second controversy or a denial of Stone’s apology.

edges.relationship: Scott rejects Palmer’s opposition between discourse and class struggle, arguing that class and gender must be analyzed together rather than chosen as competing priorities (1987).
edges.evidence_note: Discourse includes institutions and social practices, not words alone. This adds the missing reply direction to the exchange already described in edge_920; it is not a newly discovered second debate. Palmer’s own article was not freshly reread.

edges.relationship: Scott argues that Thompson’s use of experience makes class identity foundational and obscures the contested construction of gender and other differences (1991).
edges.evidence_note: She praises his transformative history while disputing its conceptual foundation. Note24 acknowledges Sewell’s different reading. This is Scott’s interpretation, not consensus; Thompson’s books remain unread here. Distinct from the mixed Ranter exchange in edge_511. In her 2024 interview, Scott also credits Thompson’s cultural account of class formation while questioning his treatment of sexual difference in language. This later qualification is separately dated; it does not claim that he ignored culture or retract her earlier critique.

edges.relationship: Scott credits Thompson’s account of working-class protest as a formative model for making popular action politically intelligible, before her later feminist critique.
edges.evidence_note: Scott’s 2009 retrospective, p. 35, explicitly names Thompson alongside Tilly. This bounded formative debt does not attribute her later gender analysis to Thompson or cancel her criticism. The 1988 chapter remains unread.

edges.relationship: Scott recalls Charles Tilly’s SSRC mentorship in social theory, quantitative methods and collective action, while resisting classifications that flattened historical process.
edges.evidence_note: Primary memoir pp. 33, 35–37, with 2024 interview corroboration. Tilly was her interdisciplinary fellowship mentor; Harvey Goldberg remained her dissertation advisor. Louise Tilly’s separate coauthorship is preserved.

edges.relationship: Hobsbawm and Scott jointly investigate shoemakers’ radical reputation, distinguishing militant action, left allegiance and worker intellectual life instead of treating the reputation as self-explanatory.
edges.evidence_note: Substantive opening of their joint “Political Shoemakers” read in the 1984 Worlds of Labour reprint, pp. 103–113, through a third-party transcription. Oxford verifies both authors and the original November 1980 article, pp. 86–114. Collaboration, not a one-way influence; original journal body and the rest of the reprint were not read.

edges.relationship: Scott credits Hunt, alongside Elisabetta Galeotti, with close readings of the complete Gender and the Politics of History manuscript.
edges.evidence_note: Scott’s own acknowledgments, printed p.ix, identify manuscript reading. This is a specific editorial contribution, not authorship or a general intellectual genealogy. Galeotti’s joint credit remains. Selected primary frontmatter transcription and its 1988 copyright statement were read; the whole book was not newly read. The host’s 2019 listing is not the original publication date.

edges.relationship: Hunt singles out Scott’s gender-and-discourse work as an especially forceful methodological example in her case for gender’s centrality to cultural history.
edges.evidence_note: Hunt’s own introduction, printed pp.18–19 and n.42, places Scott within its methodological framing. This is scholarly reception and use of an exemplary argument, not a claim that Scott generated Hunt’s empirical practice or the whole new cultural history. The cited Scott book was not newly read in full. It is distinct from Hunt’s earlier manuscript-reading contribution.

edges.relationship: Parr explicitly connects her questions about gender and class categories to Scott’s work on the politics of gender categories, among other named interlocutors.
edges.evidence_note: Parr’s own introduction to The Gender of Breadwinners, printed p.9, relates the questions posed by her two town studies to Scott and Denise Riley, alongside Mary Poovey and R.W.Connell. This supports a bounded methodological resource, not exclusive derivation or identical conclusions. Selected introduction only; the whole book and cited works were not newly read. Original 1990 publication and later reprints/digital preview remain distinct.

edges.relationship: Higginbotham places Scott’s language-and-discourse turn among feminist frameworks she found compelling but insufficiently attentive to race.
edges.evidence_note: Her 2017 retrospective, printed p.632, names Scott’s 1986 article and 1988 book before explaining her qualified dissatisfaction with feminist theory’s racial presumptions. The criticism concerns a wider body of theory, with Scott a named example, not Scott alone. This is Higginbotham’s retrospective account of the context of her 1992 intervention, not evidence of a private exchange, a 1992 direct denunciation or rejection of every Scott argument. James C.Scott’s separate infrapolitics resource is a different person.

edges.relationship: With Keith Nield, Eley challenges Scott’s portrayal of their approach as a binary choice between discourse and materialist social history, while welcoming her insistence on sexed subjectivities (2000).
edges.evidence_note: Primary printed pp. 83–84 freshly read, with preceding context on p. 82. The reply jointly credits Eley and Nield; this personal route projects their shared intervention, not an independent Eley-only argument. Their praise for Scott’s lucidity, acknowledgment of sexuality’s importance and agreement about Rancière qualify the criticism. Existing mixed debate edge_1169 remains unchanged.

edge_1127.evidence_note: Body read in full for revision 1.152 (ILWCH 57, 2000, pp. 69–75; Cambridge PDF; data/extension-2026/languages-of-class-2026-10-22/evidence-spread.md §6.3); the abstract read for 1.147 is confirmed verbatim. Eley and Nield's essay 'will surely become an indispensable assignment in introductory graduate courses because it is synthetic in many senses' (p. 69); they 'are willing to accommodate all manner of deviations from the materialist analyses … especially what some have dubbed "the linguistic turn"', so that one 'might have punned wildly and titled the Eley/Nield essay, "Assent to Discourse"' (p. 69); 'Patrick Joyce has been expelled from the fold and Kathleen Canning is now at its center' (p. 69); 'there's a tension between Eley and Nield's desires to update the old social history by detaching it from its materialist assumptions, on the one hand, and to keep writing narratives of worker political agency, on the other' (pp. 69–70); they talk of gender 'but no mention of sex, homo- or heterosexuality, and sexual difference' (p. 70); Rancière's 1983 essay is 'an important corrective to Eley and Nield' (pp. 70–71); 'They want to define class as an effect of discourse but also as "a structural attribute of societies" as if those two were contradictory. To posit them as contradictory is to misunderstand Foucault's ideas about discourse'; 'Structures come into being through discourse: Class is one way of naming, understanding, and organizing certain forms of social inequality' (p. 71); her questions 'don't exclude class, but they don't require it either' (p. 72). Eley and Nield's reply (pp. 81–86 read): 'we have some problems with Scott's ungenerous critique … It is either discourse (here signified by Jacques Rancière and Michel Foucault) or materialist social history' (p. 83), while they 'wholeheartedly applaud Scott's citation of Rancière' (p. 84). Distinct from edge_105 (the linguistic turn's critique of social history, citing her 1991 essay) and from languages_of_class → social, which carries the debate's bearing on the field. Earlier note (1.147): Publisher abstract only (ILWCH 57, 2000, 69–75); the article body is unread. Eley and Nield's essay is marked by a tension between detaching social history from "its materialist assumptions" and continuing "narratives of working-class political agency"; "By insisting that class is still the best way of analyzing inequality and mobilizing resistance to it, the authors foreclose other possibilities for thinking about contemporary politics and for writing critical history"; her questions "don't exclude class but they don't require it either". Moderate. Distinct from edge_105 (the linguistic turn's critique of social history, citing her 1991 essay). Routing qualification, revision 1.194: the specific target is the joint Eley/Nield argument, now reachable through Eley’s individual entry. Keith Nield retains equal authorial credit in the claim and sources; the target does not imply Eley-only authorship. The mixed-critic context on edge_1169 is preserved.
